subject: Business
title: Leading Organizational Change
description: A micro-lesson that makes Leading Organizational Change usable.

hook.text: 70% of organizational change initiatives fail. The reason isn't bad strategy — it's bad leadership through the change.

buildup.text: Kotter's 8-step model starts with creating urgency and building a guiding coalition before any change begins.

discovery.text: People resist change not because they're stubborn, but because they fear loss: status, comfort, competence.

twist.text: Most leaders announce change and expect compliance. Real change requires emotional buy-in, not just rational agreement.

climax.text: Quick wins are essential: small visible successes build momentum and prove the change is working.

punchline.text: People don't resist change. They resist being changed.

quiz.question: Why do 70% of organizational change initiatives fail?
options: Leaders fail to build emotional buy-in and manage people through the transition
The strategies behind the changes are always wrong
Employees are naturally resistant to any change

details.summary: Leading organizational change requires a clear vision for why change is necessary, a coalition of supporters, and systematic attention to the human emotions that make people resist. Kotter's eight-step model guides leaders from creating urgency through anchoring change in culture.
details.whyItMatters: Roughly 70 percent of organizational change initiatives fail, usually because leaders underestimate the human dimension. People resist change not because they are irrational but because uncertainty feels threatening.
takeaways: Most change initiatives fail due to neglecting the human side of change
Creating a sense of urgency is essential before people will abandon the status quo
Early wins build momentum and convert skeptics into supporters of change

faq.question: What are the biggest reasons organizational change initiatives fail?
faq.answer: Insufficient urgency leaving people comfortable with the status quo. Lack of a powerful guiding coalition to drive change. Undercommunicating the vision by a factor of ten. Failing to generate short-term wins that prove change is working. Declaring victory too soon.

faq.question: How do you get resistant employees on board with change?
faq.answer: Understand their specific concerns rather than dismissing resistance. Involve them in designing the change process. Show early wins that demonstrate benefits. Provide training and resources for new skills. Address what they personally lose and gain. Give them time while maintaining momentum.
